title: Dharma Dilemmas: Dice, the Yaksha and Sita's Trial
bigQuestion: When the epics show good people facing hard choices, what do they teach about dharma, and why do readers disagree?

story.title: One Question in the Hall
story.kicker: A queen dragged into a hall of kings asks one legal question no one can answer.
paragraphs: The great hall at Hastinapura is full of kings, elders and princes. A game of dice has gone badly wrong. Yudhishthira, the eldest Pandava and a man known for honesty, has lost his wealth, his kingdom, his brothers and himself. Then, pressed by his opponents, he stakes his wife, Draupadi, and loses her too.

Duryodhana sends a servant to bring Draupadi to the hall. She refuses and sends back a question. Then his brother Duhshasana drags her in by the hair. She stands before the elders, in grief and anger, and asks her question aloud. When Yudhishthira staked me, had he already lost himself? If he was no longer free, how could he stake me?

The hall goes quiet. Bhishma, the respected elder, says that dharma is subtle, and he cannot answer. Only young Vikarna, one of the Kaurava brothers, says she was not rightly won. Others shout him down. The Mahabharata says that when Duhshasana tries to strip her, her garment keeps growing, and she is not shamed. Many devotees understand this as Krishna's protection.

Draupadi's question is never fully answered in the hall. It echoes through the rest of the epic, and it is one reason the war happens. For centuries, readers have asked what the elders should have done, and what dharma requires when rules and justice seem to point different ways.

In this chapter you will study four hard cases from the epics: the dice game, the Yaksha's questions, Karna's divided loyalty, and Sita's trial. You will see how devotees, scholars, feminist readers and poets have read them.
story.think: Bhishma says dharma is subtle and stays silent. Is silence a way of keeping dharma, or of failing it? What would you need to know to decide?

lessons.title: How the Game Was Lost
lessons.mainIdea: In the Sabha Parva, Yudhishthira accepts a dice challenge and loses everything, including his brothers, himself and Draupadi.
reading: The *Sabha Parva*, the Book of the Assembly Hall, is the second book of the Mahabharata. It tells how Yudhishthira was crowned in a splendid hall at Indraprastha, and how his cousin Duryodhana burned with envy. Duryodhana's uncle Shakuni, a master of dice, proposed a game to win the Pandavas' wealth.

Yudhishthira felt bound to accept, because a king was expected not to refuse a challenge. Shakuni threw for Duryodhana, and the epic suggests he played with skill and deceit. Yudhishthira lost again and again: jewels, gold, chariots, lands, then each of his four brothers, then himself, then Draupadi.

Many readers point out that Yudhishthira's sense of duty trapped him. He kept a rule of honor even while it destroyed his family. The epic does not simply praise or blame him. It shows how following one *dharma*, the rule of a king, could clash with another, a husband's and brother's duty to protect.

words.d: the Book of the Assembly Hall, second book of the Mahabharata, where the dice game happens
the eldest Pandava, known for truthfulness, who loses at dice
duty, right order, the right way to act; in the epics, often a source of conflict

look.title: Stakes Yudhishthira Lost, in Order
look.cite: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta sub-parva), summarized from K.M. Ganguli's translation (1883–96)
look.prompt: Why does it matter that he lost himself before he staked Draupadi? This order is the basis of her question.

check.q: Who threw the dice for Duryodhana?
check.why: Shakuni, a master of dice, played for Duryodhana.

check.q: Why did Yudhishthira accept the game?
choices: He was sure he would win
A king was expected not to refuse a challenge
check.why: The epic presents it as a matter of royal honor.

check.q: Which book of the Mahabharata tells of the dice game?
check.why: The dice game is in the Sabha Parva; Yuddha Kanda is in the Ramayana.

lessons.title: Draupadi's Question
lessons.mainIdea: Draupadi asks whether a man who had already lost himself could stake her, and the elders cannot answer.
reading: Draupadi's question is legal and precise. Did Yudhishthira stake her before or after he lost himself? If after, he was no longer a free man. Could a man who owned nothing, not even himself, stake anyone? She asks the assembly of elders to decide by dharma.

Bhishma, the grand elder, answers that the ways of dharma are subtle, *sukshma*, and he cannot resolve the question. Scholars point out that this is one of the few places where the epic lets its wisest elder admit he does not know. Only Vikarna and later Vidura speak up for her. The others stay silent or mock her.

Modern readers, including many Indian feminist writers, see Draupadi as a woman who uses reason and law in a hall where men hold power. Devotional readers stress her faith, since many retellings say she called on Krishna and was protected. The two readings can meet: a woman who argues well and also prays.

words.d: "subtle"; Bhishma's word for dharma when he cannot answer Draupadi
wife of the five Pandavas, who asks the famous question in the assembly hall
wise uncle and counselor at Hastinapura who warns against the game and speaks for justice

look.title: Bhishma's Answer
look.text: Bhishma says that because dharma is subtle, he cannot rightly settle Draupadi's question: a man without property cannot stake another's, yet a wife is under her husband's direction.
look.cite: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta sub-parva), paraphrased from K.M. Ganguli's translation (1883–96)
look.prompt: Bhishma gives two rules that point in opposite directions. What are they? Why might the poet show a wise elder stuck between them?

check.q: What exactly does Draupadi ask?
choices: Whether Yudhishthira could stake her after losing himself
Who will be the next king
check.why: Her question turns on the order of the stakes.

check.q: What does Bhishma say about dharma?
choices: It is simple and clearly against her
It is subtle, and he cannot resolve the question
check.why: Bhishma calls dharma sukshma, subtle.

check.q: Which Kaurava brother says Draupadi was not rightly won?
check.why: Vikarna speaks up for her and is shouted down.

lessons.title: What the Silence Means
lessons.mainIdea: Readers argue about the elders' silence and about Draupadi's protection, and the scene shapes the whole epic.
reading: The Sabha Parva says that when Duhshasana tries to pull away Draupadi's garment, more and more cloth appears, and he cannot shame her. In many later retellings and in popular devotion, this is Krishna answering her call. Critical editors note that some verses of this scene vary among manuscripts, but the scene is central in how the epic is told and loved.

After the scene, blind King Dhritarashtra, frightened by bad omens, grants Draupadi wishes. She uses them to free her husbands, asking nothing for herself. Soon a second game sends the Pandavas into thirteen years of exile. The insult in the hall becomes one of the causes of the war.

Readers draw many lessons. Some focus on the danger of *complicity*, standing by while wrong is done. Some focus on Draupadi's courage and wit. Some focus on how dharma can be twisted by clever rules. The epic seems to invite all of these readings, which is one reason it is still performed and discussed.

words.d: sharing in wrongdoing by going along with it or staying silent
a scholarly text that compares many manuscripts; the Pune critical edition of the Mahabharata was completed in 1966
being forced to live away from home; the Pandavas spend thirteen years in exile

look.title: Three Lessons from One Scene
look.text: Reader A: the scene warns against staying silent while wrong is done. Reader B: the scene shows a woman's courage and reasoning. Reader C: the scene shows how devotion is answered in need.
look.prompt: Find a detail in the scene that supports each reader. Is there a detail that none of them explains?

check.q: What does Draupadi ask for when Dhritarashtra grants her wishes?
check.why: She uses the wishes to free the Pandavas.

check.q: What is complicity?
choices: Sharing in wrongdoing by going along or staying silent
check.why: Many readers see the elders' silence as complicity.

check.q: What happens after the second dice game?
choices: The Pandavas go into thirteen years of exile
check.why: The second game leads to twelve years in the forest and a year in hiding.

lessons.title: A Lake Guarded by Questions
lessons.mainIdea: In the Vana Parva, a Yaksha guarding a lake asks Yudhishthira riddles, and he answers them after his brothers fall.
reading: During the forest exile, in the *Vana Parva*, the Book of the Forest, the Pandavas grow thirsty. One brother goes to a lake to fetch water. A voice tells him to answer questions first. He ignores it, drinks, and falls lifeless. The same happens to the next brother, and the next.

At last Yudhishthira comes and finds his four brothers lying by the water. The voice speaks, a *yaksha*, a nature spirit, who guards the lake. Yudhishthira agrees to answer. The Yaksha asks many questions, about the sun, about duty, about happiness, about what makes a person wise.

This episode is often called the Yaksha Prashna, "the Yaksha's questions." It is a favorite with Hindu families and teachers, because it turns a story into a quiz about life. In the end the Yaksha is revealed as Dharma himself, Yudhishthira's divine father, testing his son.

words.d: the Book of the Forest, third book of the Mahabharata, telling of the exile
a nature spirit in Hindu texts, often guarding water or treasure
"the Yaksha's questions"; the riddle episode at the lake

look.title: Why Answer First?
look.text: Four brothers drink without answering and fall. The fifth stops, listens and answers. The voice by the lake says: answer my questions first, then drink.
look.prompt: What might the story be saying about the difference between Yudhishthira and his brothers? Think about the dice game too.

check.q: Why do the four brothers fall by the lake?
choices: They drink without answering the Yaksha's questions
check.why: Each ignores the voice, drinks and falls.

check.q: Who is the Yaksha revealed to be?
check.why: At the end the Yaksha reveals himself as Dharma.

check.q: In which book of the Mahabharata is the Yaksha episode?
check.why: The episode happens during the forest exile in the Vana Parva.

lessons.title: The Greatest Wonder
lessons.mainIdea: Asked what is the greatest wonder, Yudhishthira answers that people see others die every day yet live as if they never will.
reading: Among the Yaksha's many questions, one is the most famous. What is the greatest wonder? Yudhishthira answers: day after day, countless beings go to the house of death, yet those who remain wish to live forever. What could be more wonderful than this?

Other questions are just as pointed. What is heavier than the earth? A mother. What is higher than the sky? A father. What is faster than the wind? The mind. What, when given up, makes a person happy? Anger. The questions test wisdom about daily life rather than learning from books.

Readers enjoy how the answers turn ordinary things into lessons. Teachers note that Yudhishthira, who lost everything by keeping a rule too rigidly at dice, now shows deep practical wisdom. Some readers see this as the epic balancing its portrait of him: a flawed man who is also wise.

words.d: a question built to test cleverness or wisdom
the fact that every living being will die
good judgment about how to live day to day

look.title: The Greatest Wonder
look.text: Day after day countless creatures go to the abode of Yama, yet those who remain behind wish to live forever. What can be more wonderful than this?
look.cite: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, the Yaksha's questions, paraphrased from K.M. Ganguli's translation (1883–96)
look.prompt: Why does Yudhishthira call this a wonder rather than a mistake? What is he asking the listener to notice?

check.q: What does Yudhishthira call the greatest wonder?
choices: People see others die yet live as if they never will
The skill of Shakuni at dice
check.why: His answer is about people forgetting their own mortality.

check.q: According to Yudhishthira, what is faster than the wind?
check.why: He answers that the mind is faster than the wind.

check.q: How do some readers see the Yaksha episode in light of the dice game?
choices: It balances the picture of Yudhishthira as flawed but wise
It proves he never made mistakes
It shows he was not the eldest Pandava
It replaces the dice game in the epic
check.why: The same man who erred at dice shows great wisdom at the lake.

lessons.title: One Brother Back
lessons.mainIdea: Offered one brother's life, Yudhishthira chooses Nakula, son of his stepmother, to keep fairness between the two mothers.
reading: When the questions end, the Yaksha offers to bring back one brother. Which will Yudhishthira choose? Many would expect mighty Bhima or the great archer Arjuna, who will be needed in war. Yudhishthira chooses Nakula instead. His choice surprises the Yaksha, and it surprises many readers too.

He explains his reason. His father Pandu had two wives, Kunti and Madri. Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna are Kunti's sons, while Nakula and Sahadeva are Madri's. With himself alive, one of Kunti's sons lives. He wants one of Madri's sons to live too. Fairness to both mothers matters more to him than strength.

The Yaksha is so pleased that he restores all four brothers and reveals himself as Dharma. Readers take the story as showing that *impartiality*, being fair and not favoring one's own, is part of dharma. It is a hopeful ending in an epic full of hard ones.

words.d: fairness that does not favor one side, including one's own
mother of Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna, and also of Karna
Pandu's second wife, mother of the twins Nakula and Sahadeva

look.title: Strength or Fairness?
look.text: The Yaksha offers one life. Bhima is strong; Arjuna is a peerless archer. Yudhishthira chooses Nakula, so that each of Pandu's two wives will have a living son.
look.prompt: What does this choice show about how Yudhishthira understands dharma? Do you think it was the right choice? Give a reason from the story.

check.q: Which brother does Yudhishthira ask to be revived?
check.why: He chooses Nakula, a son of Madri.

check.q: Why does he choose that brother?
choices: So that each of Pandu's wives has a living son
check.why: He chooses for fairness between Kunti and Madri.

check.q: What value do readers draw from this choice?
check.why: His choice shows fairness that does not favor his own mother's sons.

lessons.title: The Son No One Knew
lessons.mainIdea: Karna is secretly Kunti's first son, raised by a charioteer, and he gives his loyalty to Duryodhana, who honored him.
reading: Karna is one of the most loved and debated figures in the Mahabharata. Before her marriage, Kunti bore a son to the sun god, Surya. Afraid of shame, she set the baby afloat in a river. A charioteer and his wife found him and raised him as their own. So Karna was the eldest brother of the Pandavas, though no one, not even Karna, knew it.

Karna grew into a great archer. At a tournament he challenged Arjuna, but was mocked because he was a charioteer's son and not a prince. Duryodhana stepped in and made him king of Anga on the spot. From that day Karna gave Duryodhana his *loyalty*, and he never took it back.

Readers often see Karna as a man wronged by the social order of his time. He was judged by the family that raised him, not by his skill. Many modern plays, novels and TV series in India tell his story with deep sympathy. Other readers stress that he also took part in wrongs, such as the insult to Draupadi in the hall.

words.d: Kunti's first son, raised by a charioteer, loyal ally of Duryodhana
faithfulness to a person or cause
the kingdom Duryodhana gives Karna, making him a king

look.title: Judged by Birth
look.text: At the tournament, Karna shows skill equal to Arjuna's. He is asked his lineage and mocked as a charioteer's son. Duryodhana gives him a kingdom so he may compete as a king.
look.prompt: Why might Karna feel bound to Duryodhana for life? Was Duryodhana's act kindness, strategy, or both?

check.q: Who was Karna's mother?
check.why: Karna was Kunti's son before her marriage.

check.q: Why was Karna mocked at the tournament?
choices: He was raised as a charioteer's son
check.why: He was judged by the family that raised him.

check.q: What did Duryodhana give Karna?
check.why: Duryodhana made him king of Anga.

lessons.title: Kunti's Secret, Karna's Choice
lessons.mainIdea: Before the war, Krishna and Kunti tell Karna the truth, but he stays with Duryodhana, choosing loyalty over kinship.
reading: Before the war, in the Udyoga Parva, Krishna meets Karna and tells him the truth: he is Kunti's eldest son. If he joins the Pandavas, he could be king. Later Kunti herself comes to him by the river and asks him to join his brothers. For the first time, Karna must decide knowing who he really is.

Karna refuses. He says Kunti abandoned him, while Duryodhana stood by him. To leave now would be a betrayal. But he gives Kunti a promise: he will not kill any of her sons except Arjuna. Either way, she will still have five sons. This scene has been retold in poems, including a famous Bengali poem by Rabindranath Tagore.

Karna's choice sets two kinds of dharma against each other: duty to one's blood family and duty to a friend who kept faith. Readers do not agree on whether he chose rightly. Many admire his *integrity*, even as they see that his loyalty kept him on the side of wrongdoing.

words.d: the Book of Effort, fifth book of the Mahabharata, about failed peace efforts before the war
staying true to one's word and values
a choice between two duties that cannot both be kept

look.title: Two Duties
look.text: Duty 1: to his blood brothers, the Pandavas, and to the mother who bore him. Duty 2: to Duryodhana, the friend who honored him when others mocked him. Karna keeps duty 2 and softens it with a promise to Kunti.
look.prompt: State the strongest reason for each choice. Which reason do you find stronger, and why?

check.q: What promise does Karna give Kunti?
choices: He will not kill any of her sons except Arjuna
check.why: He promises she will still have five sons.

check.q: Why does Karna refuse to join the Pandavas?
choices: He will not betray Duryodhana, who stood by him
check.why: Karna chooses loyalty to the friend who honored him.

check.q: What is a dilemma?
choices: A choice between two duties that cannot both be kept
check.why: Karna faces a dilemma between kin and friend.

lessons.title: The Fire Ordeal
lessons.mainIdea: In the Yuddha Kanda, after Rama wins Sita back, she passes through fire to prove her purity, and Agni returns her unharmed.
reading: In Valmiki's *Ramayana*, Sita, wife of Rama, is taken by Ravana to Lanka. Rama, with Hanuman and a great army, defeats Ravana to win her back. Then, in the Yuddha Kanda, the Book of War, comes a painful scene. Rama tells Sita, before others, that he has fought to clear his name, and that she has lived in another man's house.

Sita answers with dignity and grief. She says her heart was always his. She asks Lakshmana to build a fire and enters it. Agni, the god of fire, rises from the flames and returns her unharmed, declaring her pure. Rama then says he never doubted her, but that the people needed to see. This is called the *agni pariksha*, the fire ordeal.

Many devotees read the scene as a revelation of Sita's purity and strength, and as Rama bound by his duty as a king. Other readers, including many women writers, find it painful and ask why Sita had to prove anything at all. Both responses have been part of Hindu discussion for centuries.

words.d: the fire ordeal in which Sita enters fire and is returned unharmed by Agni
the Book of War, sixth book of Valmiki's Ramayana
the Sanskrit epic of Rama and Sita, credited by tradition to the poet Valmiki

look.title: Sita Answers
look.text: Sita tells Rama that her heart, which was in her power, was always his; what happened to her body when she was helpless was not her fault. Then she asks for a fire to be built.
look.cite: Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, paraphrased from Ralph T.H. Griffith, The Ramayan of Valmiki (1870–74)
look.prompt: What distinction does Sita draw between what was in her control and what was not? How does her answer show her dignity?

check.q: Who returns Sita unharmed from the fire?
check.why: Agni rises from the flames and declares her pure.

check.q: In which book of the Ramayana is the fire ordeal?
check.why: The fire ordeal follows the war, in the Yuddha Kanda.

check.q: How do many devotees read the fire ordeal?
choices: As showing Sita's purity and Rama bound by royal duty
As a sign Rama did not love Sita
check.why: Devotional readers stress Sita's purity and Rama's duty; others question the ordeal.

lessons.title: Return to the Earth
lessons.mainIdea: In the Uttara Kanda, Sita is sent away, raises her sons, and finally returns to the earth, her mother.
reading: The Ramayana's last book, the *Uttara Kanda*, continues the story. Back in Ayodhya, Rama hears that some citizens question Sita's purity. As king, he sends her away to the forest, though she is expecting a child. She finds shelter at the hermitage of Valmiki, the poet himself, and gives birth to twin sons, Lava and Kusha.

Years later, the twins sing the Ramayana at Rama's court, and he recognizes them. Rama asks Sita to swear her purity once more before the people. Instead, Sita calls on the earth, her mother, to receive her if she has been true. The earth opens, a throne rises, and Sita returns to the earth. Rama is left in grief.

Many scholars think the Uttara Kanda was added later than the core of the epic, while many Hindus accept it as part of Valmiki's work. Some retellings leave this ending out or soften it. Readers debate what it says about kingship, justice and a woman's voice, and many see in Sita's final choice an act of great strength.

words.d: the last book of Valmiki's Ramayana, telling of Sita's exile and return to the earth
the twin sons of Rama and Sita, raised at Valmiki's hermitage
a new version of a story by a later author, often with changes

look.title: A Final Choice
look.text: Asked to prove herself a second time, Sita does not argue and does not walk into fire again. She calls on the earth, her mother, and the earth takes her home.
look.prompt: How is this ending different from the fire ordeal? What might Sita's choice say about her voice at the end of the story?

check.q: Where does Sita find shelter after she is sent away?
choices: At the lake of the Yaksha
check.why: Valmiki shelters her, and her sons are born there.

check.q: How does Sita's story end in the Uttara Kanda?
choices: She enters the fire a second time
She returns to the earth, her mother
She goes to live in the Himalayas
check.why: The earth opens and receives her.

check.q: What do many scholars think about the Uttara Kanda?
choices: It is the oldest part of the Ramayana
It is part of the Mahabharata
It was added later than the epic's core
check.why: Many scholars date the Uttara Kanda later; many Hindus accept it as Valmiki's.

lessons.title: Chandrabati's Sita
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1500s the Bengali poet Chandrabati retold the Ramayana from Sita's side, one of many voices that read the epic anew.
reading: The Ramayana has been retold in many languages: Kamban's Tamil version, Krittibas's Bengali version, Tulsidas's Hindi Ramcharitmanas, and many more. One striking retelling is by Chandrabati, a woman poet of Bengal in the 1500s. She is often called the first woman poet of Bengal.

Chandrabati's Ramayana focuses on Sita's life and suffering. It spends little time on Rama's battles and more on Sita's birth, her exile and her grief. Scholars such as Nabaneeta Dev Sen have written about how her version gives women's experience a central place, and how it was sung by women in the villages of eastern Bengal.

Retellings like Chandrabati's show that the Ramayana is not one fixed text but a living tradition with many *perspectives*. Devotees, poets and feminist scholars all take part. Studying them lets students see how one story can hold reverence for Rama and Sita and also room to question and grieve.

words.d: a woman poet of Bengal in the 1500s who wrote a Sita-centered Ramayana
the point of view from which a story is told
Tulsidas's Hindi retelling of the Rama story (c. 1570s), widely recited in North India

look.title: Whose Story Is It?
look.text: Valmiki's Ramayana follows Rama's exile, war and rule. Chandrabati's Bengali Ramayana (1500s) spends much of its length on Sita: her birth, her exile, her sorrow.
look.prompt: How might changing the center of the story change what a listener feels about the fire ordeal and Sita's exile?

check.q: Who was Chandrabati?
choices: A 1500s woman poet of Bengal who wrote a Sita-centered Ramayana
The author of the Gita Rahasya
check.why: Chandrabati was a Bengali woman poet of the 1500s.

check.q: What does Chandrabati's Ramayana focus on?
check.why: Her version centers Sita's experience.

check.q: Which is a Hindi retelling of the Rama story?
check.why: Tulsidas wrote in Hindi (Awadhi); Kamban in Tamil; Krittibas in Bengali.

review.why: Draupadi asks whether a man who lost himself could stake her.

review.q: What does sukshma mean when Bhishma speaks of dharma?

review.q: What does Yudhishthira say is heavier than the earth?
